title: At the Ruler's Table and the Drunkard's Cup
summary: The words of the wise continue with warnings about the table of a ruler and of a stingy host, the fleeting nature of wealth, and moving a boundary stone to steal from orphans. A father pleads with his son to be wise, to shun gluttony, drunkenness, and the prostitute, and the chapter closes with a vivid, almost comic portrait of a man ruined by wine who can't wait for his next drink.
story: Chapter 23 sits in the middle of the section Proverbs calls the words of the wise (22:17 to 24:22), a collection of longer sayings that follows the great run of Solomon's two-line proverbs. The voice here is more personal than in chapters 10 to 22: again and again a father addresses “my son”, as in the opening chapters of the book. The concerns are those of a young man moving into adult life, perhaps into the service of powerful people: how to behave at a great man's table, how not to wear himself out chasing money, how to honor aging parents, and how to keep his appetites from owning him.
historical:
The words of the wise are closely related to an Egyptian wisdom book, the Instruction of Amenemope, which scholars usually date to the late second millennium BC (some place it somewhat later) and which was first published in the 1920s. Several sayings in this chapter have close counterparts there. Amenemope also counsels restraint when eating in the presence of an official, warns against removing the boundary marker of a field, and pictures riches making themselves wings and flying away to the sky like birds. Most scholars conclude that Israel's sages knew this Egyptian teaching and reworked it. The reworking is telling: in Proverbs, the one who defends the orphan's field is the LORD, their Redeemer (verse 11).

The settings the chapter assumes belong to an agricultural monarchy. Rulers held banquets, and officials rose or fell by the impression they made there. Land was held by families and marked by stones, and the law of Moses made moving a neighbor's boundary marker a crime under a curse (Deuteronomy 19:14; 27:17). Wine was part of daily life across the ancient Near East, and so was drunkenness; Egyptian and Mesopotamian texts also mock the drunkard.
cultural:
In ancient Israel, a family's land was its livelihood and its inheritance, meant to pass down through the generations. Widows and orphans had no adult male to defend their claim in the town gate, so shifting a boundary stone at the edge of their field was an easy, quiet theft. Verse 11 answers that fear with a family word. A redeemer (go'el) was the nearest relative, who was obliged to buy back a kinsman's land, avenge his blood, or rescue him from debt slavery, as Boaz does in the book of Ruth. The orphan who has no such relative has one after all: God himself takes up the case.

The household assumed here is one where father and mother both teach, and where honoring them in old age was a sacred duty (verse 22). The rod of discipline in verses 13 and 14 reflects a world where physical correction of children was universal and where the greater fear was a child left without correction, heading for death. Verse 30 speaks of mixed drinks, wine blended with spices or other ingredients, a practice known across the ancient world.
literary: The chapter is a string of short instructions, many built as a command followed by a reason introduced by for (verses 3, 5, 7, 11, 18, 21, 27). Addresses to “my son” break it into sections (verses 15, 19, 26). The best-known passage is the closing poem on wine (verses 29 to 35). It opens with six rapid questions, “Who has woe? Who has sorrow?”, answers them in a single line (verse 30), then moves from the attractive (wine red and sparkling in the cup) to the deadly (it bites like a snake). It ends by letting the drunkard speak for himself, and his last words are the poem's sharpest point: “When can I wake up to search for another drink?”

outline.t: At the tables of rulers and stingy hosts, and the flight of wealth
Fools, boundary stones, and the orphan's Redeemer
Instruction and discipline for a son
Do not envy sinners or join drunkards and gluttons
Honor your parents, buy truth, and beware the adulteress

doctrines.note: Wisdom here is practical self-mastery: knowing when to restrain appetite, when to stop chasing wealth, and what to hold on to. “Invest in truth and never sell it” (verse 23) pictures wisdom as a purchase worth any price.
The chapter treats the home as the school of wisdom. A child's wisdom brings joy to both parents, and the son is told to listen to his father and not despise his mother when she is old.
The LORD is the strong Redeemer of the fatherless. Human courts may miss the moved stone, but God himself takes up the case of those who have no one to defend them.

words.note: Ga'al, to redeem, and its participle go'el, redeemer. The word belongs to family law: the go'el was the kinsman who bought back land, freed a relative from slavery, or avenged a death. Calling the LORD the orphans' Redeemer in verse 11 means God acts as their nearest relative. The same word describes God's rescue of Israel from Egypt and Job's hope in a living Redeemer.

Musar, discipline or instruction. The word covers both teaching and correction, sometimes painful correction. In verse 12 it is instruction the son must apply his heart to; in verse 13 it is the discipline a parent must not withhold. For Proverbs, being teachable and being correctable are the same virtue.

Tiqvah, hope or expectation, the outcome a person waits for. Verse 18 promises that the one who fears the LORD has a future and a hope that will not be cut off. The contrast is with envying sinners, whose success looks secure but has no future.

Yayin, wine, the ordinary drink of the ancient Near East. Scripture elsewhere praises wine as God's gift that gladdens the heart, so the chapter's warning targets lingering over it and being ruled by it, not the drink itself.

christ: The picture of God as the Redeemer of the fatherless runs through the Old Testament and comes to its fullest meaning in Christ, whom the New Testament presents as the one who redeems people who could not free themselves, making them children of God and heirs. The call to buy truth and never sell it recalls Jesus' parables of the treasure hidden in a field and the pearl of great price, where a man sells everything to gain what is worth more. And the chapter's warnings about envy of sinners and the pull of appetite find their answer in the New Testament's call to be filled with the Spirit rather than drunk with wine. These are connections of theme, not predictions.

hard.q: Does this chapter teach that parents should spank their children, and does it promise it will save them?
hard.a:
Verses 13 and 14 say that striking a child with a rod will not kill him and will deliver his soul from Sheol, the realm of the dead. Readers take this in different ways. Many Christians read it as endorsing measured physical discipline, given in love and self-control. Others note that the rod was also a common image for any authoritative correction, and argue that the principle is loving, consistent discipline rather than a particular method, especially given how easily physical punishment can become abuse, which Scripture elsewhere condemns. Readers on every side agree the passage is not a license for harshness: the point is that neglecting correction is itself a failure of love.

It is also important to read the saying as a proverb. Proverbs describe how life usually goes under God, not a guarantee. The promise that he will not die is a pointed way of saying that correction does less harm than neglect, and deliverance from Sheol describes the ordinary fruit of a disciplined life, rescue from the early death folly brings. It is not a formula that saves a child's soul, and it doesn't make parents solely responsible for a grown child's choices.

questions: Verse 5 pictures wealth growing wings and flying away. Where are you wearing yourself out for something that may not stay?
The orphan has no human defender but God takes up the case. Who in your community has no one to defend them, and what would it mean to act as their redeemer?
The drunkard's last words are about the next drink. What habit, not only alcohol, promises pleasure but leaves a person searching for more?
